# Duke study: AI model detects ADHD in kids as young as 5
![](https://www.axios.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.axios.com%2FGASOhB2-vYmHoIMGD_Jzuq_Ce1E%3D%2F52x0%2Fsmart%2F2025%2F10%2F14%2F1760466688218.jpg&w=128&q=75)

![Illustration of AI elements coming out of a doctor's suit where their head should be. ](https://images.axios.com/bm4JJ1Z42JR2ublkXnD0JsYsyZU=/1920x1080/smart/2023/01/17/194508-1673984708104.jpg?w=3840)
Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios
Duke University researchers created an artificial intelligence model they say can accurately detect ADHD in 5-year-olds' health data.
**Why it matters:** That's years earlier than most kids are diagnosed, an example of how AI tools that analyze large datasets could [reshape health care](https://www.axios.com/pro/health-tech-deals/2026/03/26/health-care-ai-tools-assessment) in the coming decades.
**Driving the news:** A paper published Monday by [Nature Mental Health](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44220-026-00628-2) showed the new AI model for detecting attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder works by age 5.
  * That is "well before that diagnosis usually happens," lead author Elliot Hill, a [data scientist](https://biostat.duke.edu/) in the Duke University School of Medicine, said in a news release.


**How it works:** Researchers fed the data from 140,000 children (birth to age 9) to an AI model already trained on the electronic health records of more than 720,000 people.
  * The AI model picked up on hidden patterns in the data and could accurately predict a diagnosis across demographics like insurance status, sex and race, the paper says.


**What they're saying:** "This is not an AI doctor," study co-author Matthew Engelhard, a fellow Duke data scientist, said in the release. "It's a tool to help clinicians focus their time and resources, so kids who need help don't fall through the cracks or wait years for answers."
  * Naomi Davis, a co-author from the field of psychiatry and behavioral sciences, added that "children with ADHD can really struggle when their needs aren't understood and adequate supports are not in place."


**By the numbers:** Around [11% of American children](https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/data/index.html) are diagnosed with ADHD, according to 2022 data analyzed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  * That's 15% of boys and 8% of girls.


**The intrigue:** Just over half (54%) of U.S. children diagnosed with ADHD were taking medication, per CDC data. 
  * Meanwhile, [demand for ADHD medications](https://www.axios.com/2026/04/28/adhd-drugs-women-prescription-surge) has surged in recent years among adults, causing drug shortages at times.


**What's next:** The researchers say the model, while promising, should undergo further study before it can be used in the real world.
